title: THEY WERE ORDERED TO KILL THE BABIES. ONE WOMAN FEARED GOD MORE THAN PHARAOH.
paragraphs: THEY WERE ORDERED TO KILL THE BABIES. ONE WOMAN FEARED GOD MORE THAN PHARAOH.

Her name was Puah. She had no crown, no army, and no power to challenge Egypt. But when a king demanded the blood of innocent children, she made a choice that would echo through eternity. And her story may expose the very thing you've been afraid to stand against.
There is a kind of courage that doesn't look like courage.
It doesn't carry a sword. It doesn't stand before a cheering crowd. It doesn't announce itself with a thunderous speech.
Sometimes courage is a trembling woman standing in a room where nobody is watching, knowing that one decision could cost her everything.
And sometimes the most dangerous person in a kingdom is not the one holding a weapon.
It's the one who refuses to obey an evil command.
Her name was Puah.
And if you've never heard her name preached from a pulpit, you need to understand something.
The Bible remembers a woman whom the most powerful man in Egypt could not control.
A woman whose hands were supposed to participate in death but instead became instruments of protection.
A woman who stood between a murderous decree and vulnerable newborn children.
And here is the question that makes her story painfully personal:
What would you do if obeying God meant disappointing, confronting, or even defying someone who had the power to destroy your future?
Don't answer too quickly.
Because most of us have never stood before Pharaoh.
But almost all of us have faced something that demanded our silence when we knew the truth.
And the story of Puah begins in a place where silence had become dangerous.
Egypt.
A nation of magnificent buildings, powerful rulers, and extraordinary wealth.
But beneath its greatness was a terrible injustice.
The descendants of Israel had multiplied in the land, just as God had promised their forefathers. Yet their growing numbers frightened the new king of Egypt.
He looked at a people and saw a threat.
He looked at families and saw enemies.
He looked at children who had not even been born and imagined a danger to his throne.
Fear turned into oppression.
Oppression turned into slavery.
And when slavery failed to stop the growth of the Israelites, Pharaoh reached for something darker.
He decided to turn childbirth into an instrument of extermination.
Exodus 1:15–16 records:

"And the king of Egypt spake to the Hebrew midwives, of which the name of the one was Shiphrah, and the name of the other Puah: And he said, When ye do the office of a midwife to the Hebrew women, and see them upon the stools; if it be a son, then ye shall kill him: but if it be a daughter, then she shall live." (KJV)
Read that again.
He wasn't asking soldiers to fight an enemy army.
He was ordering midwives to kill newborn boys.
Women whose calling was to assist mothers in bringing life into the world were commanded to become agents of death.
Imagine the horror of that moment.
A mother exhausted from labor.
A child taking his first breath.
The fragile sound of a newborn cry.
And a royal command demanding that the very person entrusted to help should become the one who ends his life.

Scripture does not tell us exactly what Puah felt when she heard Pharaoh's command. It doesn't describe her facial expression, her heartbeat, or the conversation she may have had afterward with Shiphrah.
We must not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
But we know what she did.
And what she did tells us something extraordinary about the God she feared.
She refused to cooperate with evil.
Exodus 1:17 says:
"But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive." (KJV)
There it is.
One of the most quietly revolutionary sentences in the Old Testament.
The midwives feared God.
And the babies lived.
The Hebrew text begins with the words:
וַתִּירֶאןָ הַמְיַלְּדֹת אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים
Vattirena hamyalledot et-ha'Elohim.
Meaning, in context, "But the midwives feared God."
The verb comes from the Hebrew root יָרֵא (yare'), meaning to fear, to stand in awe of, or to reverence.
This wasn't merely a moment of religious emotion.
It was a conviction strong enough to govern their actions.
Puah and Shiphrah recognized an authority greater than Pharaoh.
And that changed everything.
Notice what the passage does not say.
It does not say they had enough political influence to protect themselves.
It does not say they possessed secret military support.
It does not say God gave them a written guarantee that they would survive.
It says they feared God.
And they refused.
That is the difference between a faith that exists only in our vocabulary and a faith that reaches into our decisions.
Because sometimes the real test of what we believe is not what we say during worship.
It is what we refuse to do when disobedience to God would make our lives easier.
Some people can sing about holiness on Sunday and compromise their integrity by Monday.
Some can speak passionately about truth until telling the truth threatens their position.
Some can publicly defend righteousness while privately surrendering to the very sins they condemn.
And before we judge them too harshly, we should examine ourselves.
How many times have we known what was right but remained silent because we feared losing someone's approval?
How many times have we tolerated dishonesty because confrontation felt uncomfortable?
How many times have we excused sin because repentance would require surrendering something we loved?
Pharaoh may not be standing in front of us.
But the temptation to fear human consequences more than God is still painfully real.
Puah's story asks us something we cannot easily escape.
Who has the final authority over your obedience?
The person who can reward you?
The person who can reject you?
The people whose approval you desperately want?
Or the God who gave you life?
And perhaps the most beautiful part of this story is that Puah was not alone.
Scripture names another woman.
Shiphrah.
Two names preserved in the Word of God.
Two women who stood together against a royal decree.

We should be careful here. The Hebrew expression used in Exodus 1:15 can be understood as referring to Hebrew midwives or midwives who served Hebrew women, and interpreters have discussed their precise ethnic identity. The passage does not give us enough information to settle every question about their background.
But it leaves no uncertainty about their allegiance.
They feared God.
They protected the children.
And they would not become instruments of Pharaoh's cruelty.
There is also something important about Puah's name.
In Hebrew it appears as פּוּעָה (Pu'ah).
Scholars have proposed connections between her name and sounds associated with calling or crying, but its precise etymology is uncertain.
We should not build a spiritual doctrine on an uncertain name meaning.
The power of her story is not hidden in a speculative definition.
It is revealed in what Scripture plainly records about her obedience.
She helped preserve life when the king demanded death.
And that is enough to make her name unforgettable.
But Pharaoh noticed.
The babies were still living.
His command had not produced the result he wanted.
So the king summoned the midwives.
Exodus 1:18 records his question:
"Why have ye done this thing, and have saved the men children alive?" (KJV)
Imagine being called to answer before the ruler whose command you had refused.
The biblical text does not describe the setting or the consequences they anticipated. But the danger of defying an absolute ruler is not difficult to understand.
The midwives answered that the Hebrew women were vigorous and gave birth before the midwives arrived.
Their explanation appears in Exodus 1:19.
Christians have long discussed whether this answer was entirely factual, strategically incomplete, or deceptive. The text does not provide enough information to resolve every detail.
But it does tell us why God dealt well with the midwives.
It was not because Scripture was celebrating dishonesty.
It was because they feared God and refused to participate in murder.
Exodus 1:20–21 says:
"Therefore God dealt well with the midwives: and the people multiplied, and waxed very mighty. And it came to pass, because the midwives feared God, that he made them houses." (KJV)
The Hebrew expression translated "made them houses" is commonly understood as God establishing households or families for them. The exact nature of the blessing is not described in detail.
And here we must resist a dangerous temptation.
It would be easy to turn Puah's story into a promise that every act of obedience will immediately produce financial success, a perfect family, or protection from suffering.
But that is not what the whole Bible teaches.
Many faithful servants of God suffered terribly.
Some lost their homes.
Some were imprisoned.
Some were killed.
Jesus Himself warned that following Him could bring persecution.
The blessing of obedience is not that God owes us a comfortable life.
The blessing is that we belong to Him, and our faithfulness is never meaningless before His eyes.
Puah's obedience mattered.
Even when the king opposed it.
Even when the children she protected could never repay her.
Even when history might have forgotten her.
God did not forget.
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
You have been doing the right thing for a long time.
Trying to remain honest in an environment that rewards compromise.
Trying to raise your children in the fear of God while the world pulls them in a hundred directions.
Trying to forgive someone who wounded you deeply.
Trying to walk away from a sin that once controlled your life.
Trying to remain faithful when nobody applauds your sacrifice.
And somewhere along the way, you began wondering whether any of it matters.
Whether God sees.
Whether your quiet obedience has any value.
Listen carefully.
The absence of human applause is not the absence of God's attention.
Puah was not Pharaoh.
She did not command an empire.
Yet Scripture preserves her name while leaving the Pharaoh of Exodus 1 unnamed.
The text does not explicitly explain why the names are presented that way, but the contrast is striking.
The ruler who tried to control life through death is remembered in this passage by his title.
The women who feared God are remembered by name.
Power can make a person famous for a generation.
Faithfulness can leave a testimony that speaks across centuries.
And there is another detail that makes this story even more profound.
Pharaoh's plan did not end with the midwives.
When his secret command failed, he escalated his cruelty.
Exodus 1:22 records that he commanded his people to cast every newborn Hebrew son into the river.
The threat grew.
The darkness deepened.
And then Exodus 2 introduces a Hebrew mother who hid her baby boy.
When she could hide him no longer, she placed him in a carefully prepared basket among the reeds beside the Nile.
That child was Moses.
The man whom God would later call to confront Pharaoh and lead Israel out of Egypt.
Now, we must be precise.
The Bible does not say Puah personally delivered Moses.
It does not say she knew his mother.
It does not identify a particular child whom she saved.
We cannot claim those details as facts.
But the biblical narrative places the courageous resistance of the midwives immediately before the birth and preservation of Moses.
Pharaoh was attempting to destroy Israel's sons.
God was preserving His people.
And the very child who would eventually confront Egypt's king emerged in the shadow of that murderous decree.
Do you see the irony?
Pharaoh was terrified that Israel would become too strong.
So he tried to eliminate the boys.
Yet the story moves toward the raising up of a deliverer whom Pharaoh could not ultimately stop.
The king could issue decrees.
But he could not overthrow the covenant purposes of God.
And this is where Puah's story begins pointing us toward something greater than Puah.
Because Exodus is not ultimately a story about human bravery alone.
It is a story about the God who remembers His covenant, hears the cries of the oppressed, and acts to redeem His people.
The deliverance through Moses becomes one of the great foundations of the biblical story.
But centuries later, another child would be born under the shadow of a murderous ruler.
Jesus Christ.
Matthew 2 tells us that Herod, threatened by news of a newborn king, ordered the killing of young boys in Bethlehem and its surrounding region.
The circumstances were different, and Scripture does not say that Puah's actions directly foreshadowed a particular event in Jesus' childhood.
Yet the parallel is sobering.
Once again, a ruler feared losing power.
Once again, vulnerable children were threatened.
And once again, human cruelty could not overturn God's redemptive purpose.
Jesus was preserved in His childhood.
But He did not come merely to escape the violence of sinful humanity.
He came to confront sin at its deepest root.
He came to save sinners.
He came to give His life as a ransom for many.
Puah and Shiphrah protected children from death.
Jesus Christ came to deliver His people from the dominion of sin and the final judgment it deserves.
The midwives could preserve earthly life.
Only the Son of God can give eternal life.
And this is the Gospel that makes every story of faithful courage find its proper center.
Our greatest hope is not that we can become brave enough to save ourselves. Our greatest hope is that Jesus Christ was faithful enough to save us.
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He went to the cross for sinners.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares.
He rose from the dead.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to all who repent and believe.
That means your story does not have to end where your worst decision left you.
Maybe you were not courageous when you should have been.
Maybe you stayed silent while someone suffered.
Maybe you compromised because you were afraid.
Maybe you have spent years hiding a sin that is slowly destroying your peace.
Maybe the person everyone admires is not the person you know yourself to be when nobody is looking.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But through Jesus Christ, your past does not have to dictate your eternal future.
Grace is not permission to continue in sin.
Grace is God's undeserved kindness that brings us to repentance, forgiveness, and a transformed life.
And repentance is not simply feeling terrible about what we have done.
It is turning toward God, confessing our sin, and trusting the Savior who alone can cleanse us.
The Gospel does not say, "Pretend you never failed."
It says that Christ died for sinners, and in Him there is real forgiveness.
Not cheap forgiveness.
Not forgiveness purchased by religious performance.
Forgiveness purchased through the precious blood of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps you have spent so long believing that God could never use someone with your history that you have forgotten what kind of people His grace restores.
Peter denied Jesus.
Yet the risen Christ restored him.
Paul persecuted the church.
Yet Christ showed him mercy and called him into service.
The thief on the cross had no opportunity to build an impressive record of religious accomplishments.
Yet he turned to Jesus in faith and received the promise of paradise.
Their stories are not identical.
But they testify to one glorious truth.
Jesus Christ is greater than the sin of those who turn to Him.
And the courage to obey God does not grow from pretending we are strong.
It grows from knowing whom we belong to.
Puah feared God more than Pharaoh.
For the Christian, that reverence is deepened by the knowledge that the God we fear is also the Father who has shown His love through His Son.
We do not obey to purchase His grace.
We obey because His grace is changing us.
We do not stand for righteousness to earn salvation.
We stand because salvation belongs to the Lord.
And sometimes that obedience begins with something that looks very small.
Refusing to join a cruel conversation.
Defending someone who cannot defend themselves.
Telling the truth when a lie would be convenient.
Protecting a vulnerable person even when it costs us.
Confessing a hidden sin.
Asking forgiveness.
Ending a dishonest relationship.
Returning what does not belong to us.
Choosing Christ when the world offers a thousand reasons to compromise.
These choices may never become headlines.
But they are not invisible to God.
And there is something else we must remember.
Puah did not act alone.
Shiphrah stood with her.
We were never meant to treat the Christian life as a solitary performance.
We need brothers and sisters who will encourage us to remain faithful.
People who will tell us the truth when we are drifting.
People who will pray with us when fear becomes overwhelming.
People who will remind us of Scripture when our emotions are louder than our convictions.
That is why the church matters.
That is why discipleship matters.
That is why biblical encouragement should never be reduced to content we consume and immediately forget.
Truth is meant to shape our lives.
Be honest before God.
What is your Pharaoh?
Not necessarily a person.
Perhaps it is the fear of rejection.
The approval of others.
A secret addiction.
A habit of compromise.
A relationship that keeps pulling you away from Christ.
A workplace culture where dishonesty has become normal.
Or the terrible belief that obedience is pointless because nobody notices.
You do not have to reveal private details publicly.
Not as a performance.
Not to impress anyone.
But as a simple confession that you are not ready to surrender your faith to fear.
There may be another believer reading who understands your struggle more deeply than you imagine.
Someone who has walked through the same valley.
Someone who can remind you that the Lord is near to the brokenhearted.
Someone who will pray for you instead of judging you.
And if you have a testimony of how Jesus has restored your life, share what you are comfortable sharing.
Your testimony cannot replace Scripture.
But it can point another wounded person toward the Savior revealed in Scripture.
Think about the people in your life.
The mother who is exhausted from trying to keep her family together.
The father quietly struggling with fear.
The young believer pressured to compromise.
The friend who has been wounded by religious hypocrisy.
The person who has walked away from church because they believe there is no place left for them.
The one who thinks their past is too scandalous for grace.
Someone needs to be reminded that God sees faithfulness even when the world overlooks it.
Only Jesus saves.
But because a shared message of biblical truth may reach someone who would never have searched for it themselves.
Because encouragement should not end when the screen goes dark.
It should send us back to God's Word.
Back to prayer.
Back to the fellowship of believers.
Back to the daily obedience of following Jesus.
And this is also why I want to speak to those who believe in the mission of Gospel Warrior and want to help it continue.
Every article written, every biblical resource shared, and every effort to reach another person with the message of Christ requires time, work, and resources.
We want this ministry to continue growing so that more people can encounter Scripture, understand the Gospel, and find encouragement to follow Jesus faithfully.
Not because paying for content makes you more faithful.
The grace of God is not for sale.
Salvation is the gift of God through Jesus Christ, not a reward for financial support.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
That is the heart of this invitation.
Not pressure. Partnership.
It can be part of your personal giving, but it should not be confused with a mandatory biblical tithe, a church offering, or a replacement for faithfully supporting your local church.
Your responsibility to your family, your local congregation, and those genuinely in need matters.
We never want you to give out of fear, guilt, or the belief that God will love you more if you pay.
These items are not the Gospel.
The greater purpose is not merchandise.
It is helping more people encounter the truth of God's Word.
And there is another resource I want you to know about.

These resources are intended for believers who are serious about growing deeper in Jesus Christ, studying Scripture, strengthening their prayer lives, understanding sound biblical teaching, and walking faithfully through the struggles of everyday life.
You do not need to purchase God's Word.
It is about Jesus Christ.
It is about the sinner who needs forgiveness.
The wounded believer who needs restoration.
The weary disciple who needs encouragement.
The person trapped in shame who needs to hear that the cross of Christ is sufficient.
The young Christian who needs to learn that following Jesus requires more than religious excitement.
And the person who has never opened a Bible but may begin asking eternal questions because someone cared enough to share the truth.
That is why sharing matters.
That is why teaching matters.
That is why prayer matters.
And that is why every faithful act of service, however unseen, has value when offered to the Lord.
Now return with me, one final time, to Egypt.
To a king who believed he controlled the future.
To a decree that threatened the lives of innocent children.
To two women whose names were Shiphrah and Puah.
They could not see the entire unfolding story of redemption.
They did not know everything God would accomplish in the generations to come.
They simply faced a terrible command and chose to fear God.
And centuries later, we are still reading about them.
Not because they conquered a kingdom.
Not because they became wealthy.
Not because they built monuments to themselves.
But because they refused to surrender their obedience.
And maybe that is what God is calling you to remember today.
You may not be able to change an entire nation.
You may not be able to repair every broken relationship.
You may not be able to undo the damage of yesterday.
You may not be able to silence every voice that tells you to compromise.
But by the grace of God, you can take the next faithful step.
You can repent.
You can tell the truth.
You can protect the vulnerable.
You can seek forgiveness.
You can stand for what is right.
You can trust Jesus when obedience becomes costly.
And when you fail, you can return to the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
Because Christianity is not the story of perfect people proving their worth to God.
It is the story of a holy and merciful God redeeming sinners through Jesus Christ and transforming them by His grace.
Puah's courage is worth remembering.
But Christ's saving work is worth trusting with your eternity.
So before you leave this story, ask yourself one final question.
When the moment comes for me to choose between the approval of people and obedience to God, whose voice will I follow?
Because the world may never know the names of everyone who chooses to do what is right.
But the Lord knows His own.
And when you remember Puah, remember the greater Redeemer to whom the whole story of Scripture leads.
The Savior who entered our broken world.
The Savior who carried our sin.
The Savior who conquered the grave.
The Savior who still calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His name.
Pharaoh tried to erase a generation, but God preserved the names of the women who refused to help him—and the greatest name in the story of redemption is still Jesus.
